content:
Sauvignon Blanc has been here in the U.S. for a long time. From when viticulturist Charles Wetmore, founder of Cresta Blanca Winery, imported original grape cuttings from Bordeaux’s famed Château d’Yquem in the 19th century to when Robert Mondavi coined the rich, oak-aged Fumé Blanc style in Napa Valley.

Since then, the variety has happily existed in California and eventually traveled across the various wine regions of the U.S., from the Pacific Northwest to the shores of Maryland. This year also showed us that Sauvignon Blanc is thriving in Virginia, producing expressive, balanced wines that should not be overlooked in the Savvy B conversation.

We are also witnessing a shift in its home in the Loire Valley of France. The flinty and angular years of the past still exist today, but with more texture and depth. And we must not forget Friuli, a region that embraced stainless steel tanks early, and makes some amazing wines from the grape they call simply Sauvignon.

We tasted all of it for you, and below is our curated compilation of the best of the best from the grapes’ native land to its new terroirs (including Colorado!). Here are the best Sauvignon Blancs of 2026.

Why You Should Trust VinePair

Every year, VinePair conducts dozens of tastings for our “Buy This Booze” product roundups, highlighting the best bottles across the world’s most popular wine and spirits categories.

Within this scope, VinePair’s tasting and editorial staff sample thousands of bottles every year. This ensures we have a close eye on what’s new and exciting. Crucially, it also provides us with the context needed to distinguish the simply good from the truly great, whether from a quality or value-for-money perspective — or both.

Ultimately, our mission is to offer a clear, reliable source of information for drinkers, providing an overview applicable to day-to-day buying and drinking. Learn more about VinePair’s tastings and reviews department here.

How We Taste

We believe in tasting all products as our readers typically would: with full knowledge of the producer and, importantly, the price. Our tastings are therefore not conducted blind.

VinePair’s tasting panel evaluates every wine on its aromas, flavors, structure, balance, and quality. We also consider whether or not the wine showed typicity for its specific grape or region.

How We Compiled This List

To provide our readers with the most comprehensive and thoroughly tested list of the best Sauvignon Blancs to buy, VinePair invited producers, distributors, and PR firms working on their behalf to send samples for consideration. These bottles were submitted free of charge — producers didn’t pay to submit, nor did VinePair pay for the products. All were requested with the clear understanding that submission does not guarantee inclusion in the final list.

For the Sauvignon Blanc roundup, we assigned a score to each product on a 100-point scale based upon the quality and intensity of its aromas, flavors, texture, and finish. Then we reviewed all scores and compiled an editorially driven list that meets our criteria for the best Sauvignon Blanc to buy right now. Each wine was assessed on quality, price, and availability to compile the final list.

The Best Value Sauvignon Blanc

Dogwood & Thistle Wine Company Monticello Sauvignon Blanc 2025

Owners Sandy and Erin Robertson make great wine. We’ve reviewed many cuvées from Virginia’s Dogwood & Thistle over the years here at VinePair, but this might be the best one yet. Sauvignon Blanc had an amazing vintage in the Commonwealth, with incredible quality that punches far above its price point.

This crisp expression is crafted by gently pressing the grapes and aging the wine in a combination of stainless steel tanks and neutral barrels. This helps maintain freshness while adding a layer of texture and weight to the palate. The wine opens with bright notes of freshly squeezed lemons and white pepper, while the palate delivers ripe orchard fruit and a river rock minerality.

FAQs

Which country makes the best Sauvignon Blanc?

Originally from France, Sauvignon Blanc now grows all over the world. The most notable regions for Sauvignon Blanc are California, New Zealand, Chile, Italy, Bordeaux, the Loire Valley, and South Africa.

Why is New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc so popular?

New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc has notes of tropical fruit, grapefruit, grass, and lime that make the wine easy to sip and appealing to a wide range of tastes. It also pairs well with popular dishes such as seafood and fresh vegetables.

Is Sancerre Sauvignon Blanc?

Sancerre is a region of France that showcases a crisp expression of Sauvignon Blanc grapes. Sauvignon Blanc wines from this region have notes of tart lemon, wet stone, and green apple and are known for their light flavor profile and minerality.

What’s the correct serving temperature for Sauvignon Blanc?

The best serving temperature for Sauvignon Blanc is between 45 and 49 degrees Fahrenheit. A general rule of thumb is that the lighter a wine is in color and flavor, the colder it should be served. We recommend chilling Sauvignon Blanc in the fridge for roughly an hour and a half and letting it come up to temp on the kitchen counter for 20 minutes before serving.

On Tuesday, Maker’s Mark announced the 2026 release of its Cellar Aged series. The fourth edition of this coveted, age-stated collection, Maker’s Mark Cellar Aged 2026 is a combination of 11-, 12-, and 14-year-old bourbons, each bottled at cask-strength and blended to 112.1 proof.

Maker’s Mark first debuted the Cellar Aged series in 2023 with a blend of 11- and 12-year-old bourbons, the brand’s then-oldest release to date. Last year’s release hiked up the age even further to include a 14-year-old bourbon that accounted for 16 percent of the final product. The 2026 release blends 49 percent 11-year-old, 33 percent 12-year-old, and 18 percent 14-year-old bourbons — one of the distillery’s most mature blends to date.

“What excites me isn’t really the numbers — it’s what those different ages contribute to the blend,” Maker’s Mark master distiller Blake Layfield says. “We believe that age is a number, but maturity is a quality. We’re not necessarily chasing the oldest bourbon that we can make. We’re chasing the best flavor that we can create.”

Brand tasting notes highlight dark fruit, clove, and orchard fruit on the nose. The palate opens with a sweetness of honey, brown sugar, and plum flavors, leading into a lingering finish rich in almond, baking spice, and green apple.

Maker’s Mark’s Cellar Aged expressions are aged in a warehouse before finishing maturation in a limestone cavern at the Loretto, Ky., distillery. The site’s traditional warehouses can teeter between -10 degrees Fahrenheit and 120 degrees F, but the cavern maintains a 50 degree F setting, Layfield says. The cellar’s controlled temperature helps Layfield better monitor the whiskeys’ flavor development.

“The lower temperature slows the influence of the wood while allowing the whiskey to continue to evolve,” he says. “That’s how we get that depth and that complexity, while keeping the fruit and oak in balance.”

The newest Cellar Aged release comes as many whiskey brands worldwide are leaning into age-stated expressions. Rather than going full-force into high-age whiskeys, Layfield says, the Cellar Aged blends offer him some elbowroom to experiment with how maturity and youth can interact.

“The 14-year brings extraordinary maturity and depth, but the younger bourbons bring in some of that vibrancy, fruit, and balance,” he says. “Blending is about finding the point where those things start to amplify each other.”

The whiskey will be available at select retailers nationwide starting Sept. 1 for a suggested retail price of $175, with international rollouts to begin later this year and in early 2027.

content:
As in many cities, the cocktail scene is booming in Vilnius, Lithuania, where a growing number of bars are offering world-class mixed drinks, marking a dramatic change from just a decade or so ago. But for some visitors, finding a great Martini can still be a challenge.

Greta Skamaročiūtė, head bartender at Nomads Cocktail Bar in the city’s Old Town, says that several customers have come in with a story to tell. One American couple recently shared what happened when they tried to order their favorite drink elsewhere.

“They mentioned that they went to some other place and asked for a Martini, and the gentleman got a shot of vermouth and a shot of vodka,” she says. “They were quite disappointed with the serve.”

Happily, those travelers found what they wanted at Nomads, where the menu lists five variations on the gin Martini — Dry, Dirty, Gibson, Vesper, and Truffle — among other recipes. For Skamaročiūtė, one of the co-founders of the Baltic Bar Show, it really depends on where you go.

“If it’s a good cocktail bar, you’ll definitely get a good Martini,” she says. “But they’re not in every restaurant, not in every bar, and not on every corner. You have to look for a good place.”

That’s probably true for most drinks, but the Martini seems to be a special case. Today, great options for cocktails abound across Europe, and yet you’ll still find questions about the difficulty of finding a good Martini in online travel and cocktail forums, as well as personal essays from travel writers about how much Continental versions of the drink suck.

It’s not impossible to get a well-chilled, properly stirred combination of gin and vermouth, served up, in the Old World. But for a number of reasons — from brand and ingredient confusion to taste and flavor preferences that cross national borders — it’s still not as easy as it could be.

Different Flavors, Different Strengths

With her dual role as the host of her own cocktail classes and on “My Tiny Bottles,” a podcast and video series on spirits, Tammy Coxen naturally seeks out craft cocktail bars while traveling in Europe, including on a lengthy cross-continental jaunt this summer. One big takeaway? While there are several notable exceptions, Old World drink menus don’t seem to focus on the same “boozy stirred drinks” that fueled the cocktail renaissance in places like New York and San Francisco, and which still get plenty of love in the English-speaking cocktail world.

“When I go to a bar in Europe and I look at the menu, generally speaking, the drinks tend to be on the sweeter side, they tend to have a lot of sours,” she says. “You don’t often see a Martini on the menu.”

The idea that “cocktail” generally means “something fruity, sweet, and sour” seems to cover much of the E.U. at this point, with Martini-focused bars like Barcelona’s iconic Dry Martini being exceptions that prove the rule. Of course, the European continent also includes the U.K., where the Martini has a lengthy tradition, as well as plenty of contemporary buzz, with the Financial Times declaring the dirty version “London’s new It-girl drink” last month. Outside of the British Isles, however, drinkers in Europe seem to prefer very different flavor profiles.

Dieter Moeyaert and Shanna Delfosse are co-owners of Groot Vlaenderen in Bruges, which Gault-Millau recently named Belgium’s “cocktail bar of the year.” Moeyaert says that a classic Martini just isn’t what most customers are looking for.

“The bartenders know it’s a drink, but don’t know it in their bones, and aren’t really sure of the ins and outs of it the way they are with an Aperol Spritz, a Negroni, a Radler, a Picon-Bière, or even a Mojito. It’s just another drink, and not a particularly popular one.”

“I don’t think it’s in our vocabulary when it comes to drinks for the average European,” he says. “It’s definitely not a favorite. I think Europeans usually need a little bit of juice and sugar with their alcohol.” As he sees it, very popular drinks like the Aperol Spritz and the Negroni are “diametrically opposed” to the dry, briny character of a great Martini.

That might be a contemporary preference, but it matches up with history. David Wondrich, author of “The Comic Book History of the Cocktail,” among other titles, points out that Europe never had a multi-decade “Martini cult” the same way as the U.S. did in the mid-20th century. As such, the recipe functions as a kind of “dim memory,” rather than a widely shared cultural touchstone.

“The bartenders know it’s a drink, but don’t know it in their bones, and aren’t really sure of the ins and outs of it the way they are with an Aperol Spritz, a Negroni, a Radler, a Picon-Bière, or even a Mojito,” Wondrich says “It’s just another drink, and not a particularly popular one.” In his experience, modern European craft cocktail bars, century-old institutions, and large hotel bars generally make excellent Martinis. In other venues, the odds might be against you.

Moeyaert says that Groot Vlaenderen generally serves only about one classic Martini per day, usually to someone who is speaking English, not Dutch or French.

“I would say only people from the U.K. and Americans drink it,” he says. “Most Europeans stay away from it, because it’s pretty strong.”

This summer, Moeyaert and Delfosse traveled to the U.K., sampling great Martinis at storied specialty bars like Dukes.“The waft of the alcohol meets you in the lobby as you enter the bar,” he says. “It’s so strong, your day is finished if you have one.”

At Nomads, the relative strength of the Martini has even led to a new menu option. The bar’s five classic Martinis are all made with 60 ml (2.11 oz) of Tanqueray No. 10, which has a relatively brawny 47.3 percent ABV, served in a 6:1 ratio. However, every Martini can also be ordered in a “Tiny” portion, served at half the size, for exactly half the price.

“The main reason was educational, because of course, we noticed it’s not a very popular drink here,” Skamaročiūtė says. “We wanted to have a less intimidating way of drinking a Martini, with an option to try more than one without getting wasted, and without having regrets if you realize the drink is not for you and you just can’t finish it.”

What “Martini” Means

If the wrong taste profile and too much booze are two strikes against the Martini’s popularity in Europe, another might be the power of the Martini brand a.k.a. Martini & Rossi, as well as the widespread tradition of drinking vermouth on its own. Originally founded in Turin, Italy, the company’s vermouth has been a favorite standalone tipple in many European countries for over 150 years. Today, the one-word “Martini” logo is ubiquitous on beach umbrellas, awnings, menus, and table tents across the Continent. As such, if you ask for a Martini at a non-specialist bar, café, or restaurant in many cities, you’re very likely to get a chilled (but not super-cold) glass of Martini Extra Dry, ungarnished, with no other spirit. For a lot of people in Europe, the very word “Martini” means vermouth — not gin, vodka, or something in a V-shaped glass.

The strength of that brand even means that customers are confused about other contemporary drinks with Martini in the name, Delfosse notes.

“It’s definitely not a favorite. I think Europeans usually need a little bit of juice and sugar with their alcohol.”

“A lot of people ask, ‘Is there Martini vermouth in the Pornstar Martini?’” she says. With Groot Vlaenderen’s customers generally looking for “something fruity or more on the sweeter side,” that would be unwelcome, in contrast to the preferences she encountered while sampling Martinis in London this summer. “They like their brine in the U.K.”

In addition, there’s another hermeneutic angle to the Martini’s lack of appeal across Europe. For many, the strength of the drink, its long-term association with James Bond, and lore about the Martini-fueled Rat Pack all combine to cast the Martini in a macho light. By contrast, European cocktail culture can be seen as coming from a very different place.

Or, to quote Dril: This whole thing smacks of gender.

“Martinis in the U.S. were always male-coded, right? It’s men that went out for three-Martini lunches, not women,” Coxen says. “They’re very male-coded, whereas male-coded drinking in Europe is beer. I think that cocktails are more coded ‘women’ in Europe, still, than in North America.”

As such, Skamaročiūtė, Delfosse, and other women in the European drinks industry might be the ones who finally elevate the classic Martini in the Old World. Skamaročiūtė describes the drink as a kind of “final level” for drinkers, who start out by sampling various sweet-and-sour drinks. As an intermediate step, they might move on to the Negroni, whereby they start to appreciate bitterness.

“Then, after you try a lot of things, you can ask for a Martini and actually enjoy it,” she says. “You basically just develop your flavor palate for simpler flavors that are not as loud.”

Delfosse says that a future winter menu at Groot Vlaenderen will feature the Martini more prominently, including a version garnished with blue-cheese-stuffed olives. Her own preference is for a 7:1 ratio, with a dash of orange bitters and a twist.

An olive is acceptable, she says, but no brine, please.

“I love the Martini,” she says. “The dryer, the better.”

content:
Check out our list of the most underrated red wines here!

Often with plush, fruit-forward qualities or big, bold structures, red wines tend to carry a connotation of luxury. With that reputation comes hefty price tags, but like in any genre of wine, sometimes the liquid itself doesn’t live up to the bottle’s status.

But it’s not always easy to differentiate which pricey bottles are all for show and which are actually worth the hype. That’s why we asked sommeliers from around the country to name the grapes, regions, or producers that they think fall a bit flat compared to their sky-high reputations. Naturally, many mention the typical calling cards for “luxury red” and explain why they aren’t always up to snuff. To steer you in the right direction, the pros point toward alternative options to try that deliver similar qualities but with more finesse and cheaper prices.

While every consumer has their own preferences, it’s often helpful to do some research before splurging on a big-name bottle. With that said, these are the most overrated red wines, according to 11 sommeliers.

The most overrated red wines, according to sommeliers:

  • Amarone della Valpolicella
  • Left Bank Bordeaux
  • Rioja
  • Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Pinot Noir
  • Mass-produced California Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Argentine Malbec
  • Napa Cab
  • California Zinfandel
  • Expensive reds for expensive’s sake

“I think Amarone della Valpolicella is one of the great red wines of the world and a star of Veneto, but where it can be overrated is that there are only a handful of producers that I trust to consistently deliver quality. It’s not the easiest wine to make and it can get hot (meaning high alcohol) easily in unskilled hands. Making it requires drying the grapes on mats for up to four months to concentrate the sugars, but that can lead to residual sugars in some wines. These wines aren’t cheap either and sometimes they lack the freshness of the ones made in skilled hands. While I love Amarone della Valpolicella, I’m skeptical about which ones will live up to the hype (and price point).” —Andrew Principe, owner and wine director, Dirty Dime Productions, New Orleans

“The most overrated red to me is a big, bold red like a Left Bank Bordeaux. They have their place, but so many are priced to slay you and they don’t impress me at all. Winemakers need to be less rigid in their styles if they want to succeed in the evolving wine landscape. Super tannic big wines are not doing well with our customers, especially in the summertime. Although I think all well-made wine is beautiful, those are the ones that aren’t taking up any space on our shelves.” —Cassondra Bird, co-founder and beverage director, The Scout Wine Bar, Gresham, Ore.

“While painful to admit, the wines of Rioja would by my vote for most overrated. Once considered an underrated region for ageable reds at a value, the blossoming of Spanish wine in the popular consciousness has led to a ubiquity of young, mass-produced Riojas that lack character and a sense of place. Does the region still make great wines? Yes. Is there a lot of history behind the DOCa classification? Absolutely. Yet the region’s fame has overshadowed other dynamic red wine regions in Spain and cannibalized their ability to find an audience. I’ll still drink and recommend quality Rioja for its consistency and steadfast adherence to traditional methods, but I find the reds of other regions, particularly Galicia, to be a little more exciting and representative of the people and place that produce them.” —Brian Sturgulewski, beverage director and partner, Bonhomme Hospitality, Chicago

“Every grape variety is capable of producing extraordinary wines in the right place and the right hands. But if I had to choose the most overrated red grape, it would be Cabernet Sauvignon. The grape itself isn’t to blame. The problem is how it has been treated. Too often, producers have chased power over balance with heavy oak, high alcohol, and excessive extraction overshadowing Cabernet Sauvignon’s true character. Then, there is the price: Few grapes command such inflated prices regardless of where they are grown. While the greatest Cabernets deserve their legendary status, too many bottles are priced on the grape’s prestige rather than what’s actually in the glass. At its best, Cabernet is one of the world’s noblest grapes. We just need to let it be itself again.” —Dimitrios Karagiannis, wine director, Babbo, New York City

“I think Pinot Noir is a little overrated. I love it — we pour a ton of it — and yes, it makes some of the world’s most thought-provoking wines. But if you love Pinot Noir, there are so many other wines you’ll find just as compelling, and they might even save you a few dollars. Let me steer you toward Gamay from Beaujolais or the Willamette Valley, Frappato from Sicily, Trousseau from eastern France or California, or Grenache/Garnacha from France, Spain, or the United States. Next time you find yourself craving Pinot Noir, try something new instead!” —Andrew Boulton, wine director, Beckon, Denver

“This is always a touchy subject, but in my opinion, the most overrated red wine style is overly-extracted, mass-produced, heavily-oaked California Cabernet Sauvignon. Cabernet Sauvignon is one of the world’s most versatile grapes and can produce some of the best wines around. However, when the focus shifts too heavily toward ripeness, oak, and power, the wine loses the freshness, elegance, and sense of terroir that make it truly exceptional.” —Juan Gargano, sommelier, Amasa, NYC

“I think most Argentine Malbec is overrated. There are some great producers out there, but the category exploded so fast to meet demand, and at the same time, prices rose along with that demand. I don’t think all that’s out there right now has a value that matches the price. Instead, I’d point people toward Cahors, Malbec’s OG home in southwest France. Here, the wines have more structure and earthy minerality you don’t find in most Argentine Malbecs. It’s also still a well-kept secret, and the pricing is great!” —Amy Racine, beverage director and partner, JF Restaurants, NYC

“One of the most overrated categories of wine on the market today is Napa Cabernet Sauvignon. Although there are great Napa Cabs that exist from exceptional producers, these wines have become overpriced and inaccessible. I prefer a beautifully made wine from a region in Spain rich in tradition that produces bombshell red wines, such as Ribera del Duero or Rioja. These reds boast bold fruit character, earthy undertones, and layered complexities from oak aging. They can be aged in bottle for years or enjoyed right away with a delicious meal, all the while delivering a similar ‘bold red’ experience at a fraction of the price.” —Eliza Perkins, wine program manager, La Jetée, Baltimore

“California Zinfandel: It has gotten too jammy, too extracted and climate change hasn’t helped the cause. There are still some stalwarts like Ridge and Turley that I can rely on, but unless I’m eating barbecue or a burger, I just don’t want Zinfandel. Branch out and try some reds from Douro or Alentejo in Portugal for a fraction of the price. If you’re feeling adventurous try a Sankt Laurent from the Burgenland or a Teran from Friuli or Croatia.” —Alex Romero, wine buyer and educator, La Petite Grocery, New Orleans

“I don’t think any red wine is inherently overrated. What is overrated is the idea that the best bottle is always the most expensive one. Yes, you can spend thousands of dollars on what’s arguably the greatest red wine ever made, but who are you drinking it with, and where? Years from now, you’ll remember the conversation, the people around the table, and how that bottle made the moment feel. Cabernet Sauvignon often becomes the default choice, but that can keep people from discovering wines with just as much character, energy, and a stronger sense of place. My philosophy has always been to create opportunities for discovery by championing smaller producers, overlooked regions, and the stories behind the people making the wine. When guests choose curiosity over familiarity, they’re often rewarded with unforgettable bottles and experiences. That’s where the real magic of wine begins.” —Elishca Charles, general manager, Kann, Portland, Ore.

“I know someone (my dad) will strongly disagree with me, but Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon falls so short for me, especially considering the premium prices required to find a quality bottle. I will admit there are some remarkable AVA and sub-appellations that produce some incredible Cabernet, but again you’re starting to reach the point where you’ll spend serious money. On a more personal note, I also think the world has been so conditioned to drink Napa Cab, when in reality what they want is Syrah! That’s right, I said it. People aren’t as in favor of tannin as they may think; Syrahs are just softer, the fruit is more prominent, and those peppery notes are absolute perfection!” —Alex Cuper, director of beverage and hospitality, El Che Steakhouse & Bar and Brasero, Chicago

Ground Signal — which provides artificial intelligence-powered data to help beverage-alcohol brands to boost their on-premise sales — surveyed 37,471 Old Fashioneds at 26,755 cocktail venues across the U.S. to compare the state-by-state average price for the cocktail.

Perhaps surprisingly, Nevada has the highest average price for an Old Fashioned of all states at $17.51 — and the only to reach above $17. (Do Las Vegas tourists have an affinity for the whiskey cocktail? Probably: The city’s old-timey, Rat Pack-y ambiance is cause for such a classic drink.) Behind Nevada are Hawaii at $16.92, New York at $16.32, and Vermont at $16.28. Utah, where the whiskey cocktail goes for $15.95, rounds out the top five priciest states for Old Fashioneds.

The average cost for the classic cocktail across the entire U.S. is $14.38, and 21 states recorded a mean price above the national average.

So which states offer the best deal? Wisconsin is the least-expensive state for a whiskey Old Fashioned at $10.75 — even though the state is more well known for its own brandy-spiked take on the drink. Just above it are Nebraska ($11.38) and Mississippi ($11.49). Iowa and Oklahoma finish off the five cheapest states for an Old Fashioned at $11.80 and $11.89, respectively. content:
For bartenders, the idea of sustainability isn’t limited to what goes in the glass and how it gets there. Stability and community are also critical pillars to ensure hospitality professionals have long and flourishing careers. Pave the Way is a first-of-its-kind cocktail competition created by the nonprofit organization Another Round Another Rally, supported by storied cognac brand Hennessy, to help build and strengthen bartending communities, provide education about cognac and its environmental impact, and mentor bar professionals.

“We couldn’t ask for a better partner,” said ARAR’s Amanda Gunderson of the organization’s relationship with Hennessy. “They truly believe in investing in people, supporting the future of hospitality, and creating opportunities that have a lasting impact. That shared commitment makes this partnership such a natural fit.”

Northern California’s Hennessy Ambassador Zahra Bates says Hennessy’s role in Pave the Way is more than that of a symbolic sponsor. “Sustainability isn’t just about, saying ‘OK, now I’m going to recycle.’ [Hennessy’s] goal is to, by 2030, be at that 100% level and be that shining beacon for what it is to be sustainable in Cognac production.”

She goes on to explain, “[For bartending] it’s also about creating a sustainable network that you are connected with, about creating a sustainable community, both that you come from and that you want to give back to, and then also creating a sustainable career in the industry… we didn’t want to say, ‘Oh, we just recycle the husks.’”

The Competition

Pave the Way 2026 was open to bartenders across the United States and organized into seven regional areas. It kicked off with two online education sessions: one covering the history and production of cognac with the Hennessy brand, the other dedicated to sustainability. These were followed by an essay contest and a cocktail recipe submission.

Enthusiasts might be familiar with classic cognac cocktail recipes such as the French 75, Sazerac, Sidecar (and its more sugar-coated cousin the Crusta), Vieux Carré, and the Georgia Mint Julep (a precursor to the bourbon classic) among others. PTW contestants were inspired by these classics but encouraged to put their own spin on them, through the lens of sustainability.

After the submissions were reviewed, 10 finalists were selected from each region to compete locally before a live panel of judges, held in San Francisco, Los Angeles, Chicago, Miami, Atlanta and New York City. To emerge as the winning representative from their region, each cocktail was judged on how it showcased the key spirit (either Hennessy V.S. or Hennessy V.S.O.P.), represented themes of sustainability, originality, preparation/technique, and of course flavor.

The seven winners were then flown to this year’s Tales of the Cocktail for the Pave the Way Showcase where they served their unique creations for a crowd – each bartender behind their own booth that spotlighted the specific ingredients in their cocktails. This was an opportunity to share what they created for their peers at one of the biggest gatherings of mixologists from across the country, and the perfect way to grow their own networks.

Continued Brand & Sustainability Education

Following Tales, the seven will continue their career development, education, and the important conversation surrounding sustainability with Hennessy. They will dive deeper into the multiple meanings behind “cognac” and experience the care and thoughtfulness that goes into each bottle of the iconic liquid.

“Hennessy is driven by a genuine commitment to quality and innovation,” says Gunderson. “Their ethos is rooted in respect for the environment and the terroir, so sustainability isn’t just something they talk about; it’s embedded in how they approach everything they do.”

100% of the growers that Hennessy works with in Cognac are certified level 3 HVE (Haute Valeur Environnementale) low impact, and plan to be completely herbicide free in the next couple of years. In addition, Hennessy has replanted 4,500 hectares of forest and has over 300 active beehives—in a region that was years ago facing a catastrophic drop in the bee population.

It’s these guiding Hennessy principles of sustainability and community that the seven Pave the Way winners will experience during their trip to Cognac – an education they’ll be able to carry with them in their careers as they return home.

The Takeaway

Another Round Another Rally has long been committed to boosting the bartending and hospitality community and Pave the Way, supported by Hennessy, is yet another example of how they enrich the community, not just promote it.

Says Bates: “You’re going to be growing more and faster if you are actually creating your network here and with them. I found that to be a really wonderful shared value that both Another Round Another Rally and Hennessy have.”

After all, bartending isn’t just about serving guests and making delicious cocktails. The most dedicated bartenders are able to transfer their skills in meaningful ways beyond the bar. “Just because you don’t feel like you’re where you want to be at the moment doesn’t mean you’re not going to get to where you need to be,” says Bates with a note of encouragement. “You could also get further than you could have imagined.”

Bartending is a career that can be explored from different angles and last for decades. Sometimes it just takes someone to help pave the way.

content:
When considering the name “Rolling Rock,” beer fans might associate the brand with hair-flipping, guitar-smashing rock and roll. But the music genre didn’t emerge until the 1950s, and the story of Rolling Rock begins much earlier.

Rolling Rock was first produced at the Latrobe Brewing Company — a brewery founded in 1839 in Latrobe, Penn. At first, the brewery produced two labels, Latrobe Old German and Latrobe Pilsner, until a quintet of brothers took over and debuted Rolling Rock in 1939.

The extra pale lager has joined the ranks of America’s most iconic beer labels. Rolling Rock is perhaps most known for its signature green glass bottles and the number “33” embossed onto each bottle. (More on that later.) From that mysterious code to the brand’s contemporary branding, here are seven things to know about Rolling Rock.

  1. The Tito family bought the brewery that first produced Rolling Rock during Prohibition.

    The Latrobe Brewing Company’s facility went up for sale upon the onset of the 18th Amendment, and while many saw Prohibition as the end of America’s alcohol industry, five brothers of the Tito family took a chance on the return of the booze business in America. In 1932, when Prohibition was still in place, the brothers purchased Latrobe Brewing Company, and upon repeal in 1933, re-started production of the brewery’s old labels. Six years later, they decided to launch their own beer: Rolling Rock. In the decades that followed, the company underwent a number of changes in ownership, finally landing in the hands of Anheuser-Busch. The macro-brewing giant picked up the brand in 2006 before becoming Anheuser-Busch InBev in 2008.

  2. No one knows what the mysterious code means.

    The meaning behind the “33” on each bottle of Rolling Rock remains ambiguous: Even the brand’s website says, “Nobody knows.” However, that mystery has spurred a number of theories of what “33” could refer to. Some believe it’s a nod to the 33 steps involved in making beer, others purport it alludes to Rolling Rock’s brewing temperature, 33 degrees Fahrenheit. Additional theories suggest it hints at the year Prohibition was repealed, the number of stairs at the original brewery, among others.

  3. Rolling Rock once used an atypical brewing vessel…

    Since its debut Rolling Rock historically brewed and stored its beers in glass-lined tanks — unusual vessels for beermaking. Whereas most brewers use stainless steel unitanks for brewing, the original tanks insulated with glass helped reinforce the pale lager’s crisp, clean profile. Anheuser-Busch mostly ended the tradition in 2015, pivoting much of Rolling Rock’s production to steel tanks — though it still maintained the glass-lined tanks for its canned beers.

  4. … that inspired another motto embossed onto every bottle.

    The longstanding tradition of the glass-lined tanks is also featured in a pledge printed on every bottle. It reads: “Rolling Rock — From the glass lined tanks of Old Latrobe, we tender this premium beer for your enjoyment as a tribute to your good taste. It comes from the mountain springs to you.” (That motto is also 33 words, which is another theory for the meaning behind that ever-elusive number.)

  5. The brand launched a poster series to highlight visual artists.

    Rolling Rock launched a rollout of posters in collaboration with artists in 1998. The collection, titled “Rolling Rock Poster Series,” includes a number of late-’90s and early-2000s designs in a range of styles, including pop art and abstractionism. Many of the “vintage” posters are available for resale today.

  6. Rolling Rock also hosted five alternative rock music festivals.

    From 2000 to 2005, Rolling Rock hosted an annual alternative rock music festival called the Rolling Rock Town Fair. It drew some of the hottest names in early-aughts rock personalities and swarms of energetic fans to Pennsylvania’s Westmoreland Fairgrounds, just 10 miles from the beer’s birthplace in Latrobe. The Red Hot Chili Peppers headlined the inaugural festival with appearances from Moby, Fuel, and other bands. Later years’ performers included Disturbed and Stone Temple Pilots. Each year, it was a sort of mecca for Western Pennsylvania’s angsty teens, who’d bathe themselves in mud before joining the mosh pit.

  7. Rolling Rock shot for the moon in a false advertisement.

    After acquiring the brand in 2006, Anheuser Busch angered Rolling Rock devotees by shifting its production from Pennsylvania to its macrobrewery in Newark, N.J. As a result, sales began to slump, and to win back favor with fans, the brand launched an ad campaign called “Moonvertising.” Rolling Rock claimed on March 21, 2008, it would project its logo onto the moon with a laserbeam. It was a feat they obviously could not accomplish, further disappointing supporters and keeping the brand in the doghouse for some time.

content:
There’s a line in John Steinbeck’s “East of Eden” that seems to sum up our collective attitude toward the state of California winemaking today: “It never failed that during the dry years the people forgot about the rich years, and during the wet years they lost all memory of the dry years.”

While it’s no surprise that, over the nearly 300-year history of winemaking in California, it has had its own rich years — vintages of critical acclaim, recognition through events like the Judgement of Paris — and dry years –– periods of oversupply and bulk-wine glut. And yet we seem to have lost the thread on both ends. Not only have we forgotten what made California wines so celebrated in the first place, but we have also failed to reclaim our sense of pride and excitement for what winemaking in California could be.

Today, the image of California wine that most drinkers carry is ripe and heavily extracted, made with an emphasis on production and promotion, on scale and consistency. As Kae Whalen, wine director at Los Angeles’ Little Fish explains, “The monolith of overproduced, overwrought Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon, the idea that there’s an inherently lower quality of wine than what you can find in Europe… it obscures what’s really special about winemaking in the state for many drinkers.”

What that generalization overlooks is that the qualities that first made California a world-class wine growing region haven’t disappeared. If anything, Napa and Sonoma’s ocean-influenced climate, biodiverse terroir, and mix of volcanic and alluvial soils remain as compelling as ever. “Wine made in California has only become more interesting, more diverse, with as much room for classicists as for the avant-garde,” Whalen adds.

Early advocates for lighter expressions of California wines have laid the groundwork for the next generation. In 2011, a small group of winemakers led by Raj Parr and Jasmine Hirsch, of Hirsch Vineyards, created the In Pursuit of Balance (IPOB) movement, which was founded on the belief that grapes like Pinot Noir and Chardonnay could shine in California when treated with the same nuance and finesse long associated with Burgundy.

Although the group officially disbanded in 2016, their legacy carries on through some of the state’s most exciting producers today. These winemakers aren’t necessarily inventing a new California so much as carrying forward an ethos that IPOB helped reinvigorate: wines that speak to the land and history from which they come, with less intervention in the cellar and a greater emphasis on farming, balance, and the quality of the fruit itself.

That philosophy, however, comes with its challenges. “Making wine in California, particularly within the natural wine world, is becoming increasingly difficult,” explains Tatiana Ettensberger, co-owner and beverage director of Wilde’s in L.A.’s Los Feliz neighborhood. Large Napa estates control so much of the land and fruit, and climate change continues to make conditions more and more impossible.” She has a deep reverence for the renegades who, despite these hurdles, remain optimistic about California’s future. “The commitment these winemakers have to working without [additives] is genuinely courageous, and deserves far more recognition than it receives.”

Even through some of the state’s “dry years,” the future of California winemaking looks incredibly rich. And sommeliers are taking note. Wine lists that once prioritized bottles from Europe are now finding ways to make room for both long-standing new wave wineries like Hirsch, Bedrock, and Arnot-Roberts as well as labels on the rise. So we asked sommeliers which new producers they’re most excited about right now. Here are the nine winemakers defining the next generation of California wine, listed in alphabetical order.

Dorsal Wines

Dorsal Wines is the small project of Devin Alexander Myers and Jenna St. George, producing zero-additive wines along the Mendocino coast. After several years working with his mentor, Caleb Leisure, and fellow winemaker Pete Bloomberg in a shared cellar in Cloverdale, Myers relocated to the tiny hamlet of Elk Ridge in 2025, where he now makes wine out of a modest cellar just steps from his home. Meyer’s approach to winemaking is one Wilde’s Ettensberger deeply reveres. Working out of a refurbished redwood barn, Myers vinifies hand-harvested fruit from organically farmed, dry-farmed family vineyards scattered throughout the coastal valleys and ridges of Mendocino County. Myers favors short macerations, field blends, and co-ferments, typically bottling the wines young before allowing them to rest for an additional six to nine months prior to release, which varies each year. Its 2022 “Orb” — 100 percent foot trodden, whole cluster Grenache from the Sierra Foothills — is a shining example of what Dorsal does best — balancing fruit with reductive notes of flint and stone. Fermented without additives exclusively in stainless steel, the wines from Dorsal are equally esoteric as they are approachable, pushing against convention while remaining deeply tied to California’s unique history and terroir.

Emme Wines

When Rosalind Reynolds started Emme Wines in 2018, she did so with an acute awareness and appreciation for the vast community of producers and people that came before her. Named for her grandmother, Rosalind pays homage to the past and paves way for a new future in everything she does. After spending some time abroad in France, she returned to her native California as the assistant winemaker to Pax Mahle of the legendary Pax Winery in Sonoma. In addition to her work with Pax, she started her own label focusing her efforts on grapes like Colombard, Carignan, and Zinfandel — all of which have deep roots in California’s winemaking history, but fly under the radar in the modern wine scene. “It’s an incredible project that showcases wines made with a lot of spirit and care,” Camille Lindsley, owner and sommelier of East Village restaurant HAGS, shares. “Rosalind is also sourcing from really cool sites throughout California. She is working with a lot of classic but not ubiquitous grapes and styles. — her ‘You’re Lucky You’re So Cute’ Zinfandel clocks in at a lean and bright 12 percent ABV! — that showcases a cool reverence for old school California tradition with a fresh approach.”

Lady of the Sunshine

Gina Giugni, a second-generation biodynamic farmer based along the San Luis Obispo Coast, began Lady of the Sunshine in 2017 as a personal project out of deep reverence for the land she calls home. Starting out by leasing small vineyard plots, Gina and her husband, Mikey Giugni — winemaker behind partner wine brand Scar of the Sea — bought Bassi Vineyard, a 29-acre estate one mile from the ocean built on sandstone rich soils, in 2024 from California wine veteran Mike Sinor. They are in the process of converting the land to biodynamic certified farming, all the while continuing to work without pesticides in the fields or additives in the vineyard. Hannah Harrington, sommelier at Smithereens in NYC’s East Village notes, “Though she is a meticulous farmer, Gina’s wines are approachable and easy to love — the Edna Valley Pinot Noir has been a favorite of mine to sell recently.” Though the Scar of the Sea and Lady of the Sunshine wines have been industry favorites for a few years, the acquisition of this hallmark vineyard is a strong signal for the future of the growing SLO Coast AVA. And with this breezy, cool-climate approach, Giugni promises to be in a new class of winemakers challenging our conventional understanding of California white wines.

Llewelyn Wine

Pete Bloomberg, founder of Llewelyn Wine, is “a bit of a mad scientist,” according to Wilde’s Ettensberger. A somewhat elusive character, and very punk rock, Bloomberg founded Llewelyn as a one-man project in Cloverdale, Calif. in 2021. Tending to a few acres of Chardonnay in Sonoma himself, he sources the rest of his grapes from close friends and local organically farmed vineyards primarily in Mendocino. Where the range, scale and output of Llewelyn Wines varies — somewhat significantly — year to year, there are a few things Bloomberg never negotiates on, namely that his wines are never sulfured, fined, or filtered. Experimenting with style and blends, Llewelyn cuvées have included a semi-untopped Chardonnay, a rosé of old vine Carignan, and a solera style rosé. “His approach to wine has shown a perfect tension between exacting precision and a distinctly punk sensibility. Red-white blends that defy categorization, lean, coastal Pinots, long elevage Chardonnay that could be described as California’s answer to Burgundy all come to mind,” Whalen adds.

Madson Wines

Before Cole Thomas was a winemaker, he was a California farmer with a deep love for the land on which he was raised. Beginning his career as an organic vegetable farmer, he later worked as an edible landscaper and manager of the Demeter Seed Library, before finding his way to viticulture while working for Jeff Emery of Santa Cruz Mountain Vineyard. The experience set him on a path toward winemaking, first in Australia and then in New Zealand, before returning to his native Santa Cruz to launch Madson Wines in 2018. Shaped by his background in agriculture and the low-intervention winemaking techniques he learned abroad, Thomas brings an earnestness and delicacy to his wines. Rafa García Febles, general manager of NYC’s acclaimed Kabawa and Bar Kabawa, enjoys recommending bottles from Madson to showcase how the Santa Cruz Mountains are capable of remarkably expressive, balanced wines. Madson focuses on refined, terroir-driven takes on Pinot Noir, Syrah, Chardonnay, Chenin, and beyond. And its single-vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon is a far cry from the overripe California Cabernets of yesteryear — tannic yet smooth, with notes of black pepper, oregano, moss, and warm spice balanced by the tartness of blackberry and plum.

Marioni Wines

Dan Marioni is a fifth generation winemaker with deep roots in Sonoma’s winemaking history. His goal: to preserve this tradition by bringing vineyard sites across the region back to nature in order to make the best, most honest wines. “Dan is truly Sonoma’s son, born, raised, and dedicated to California’s classic expressions of Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, and the rest, but with a reverence for a more radical process of getting there,” Whalen shares.

Getting his start with Nic Coturri, son of Tony Coturri who is largely credited with leading California’s natural wine renaissance in the 1970s, Marioni launched his own project in 2019, guided by the Coturri ethos: nothing added or taken. In fact, Whalen particularly loves his ‘Fracaso’ cuvée from 2021, an homage to the last wine he made at the Coturri estate made with a classic California blend of Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Zinfandel. Today Marioni harvests nearly five acres of vines from small plots scattered across the Sonoma Coast. There is artistry in every detail of Marioni’s wines. The labels are hand-made through linocut prints that Marioni makes with his wife Jessie, a tattoo artist in the region.

R. O’Neill Latta Wines

Without any background in wine to speak of, Riley O’Neill Latta started making wine in 2019. A Malibu native, Latta was drawn back to southern California during the pandemic after having graduated from NYU and living in New York as an artist. Back in L.A., he found himself drawn to the abandoned vineyards scattered near the beaches where he had grown up surfing. Once home to a thriving wine industry, vineyards in L.A. began gradually disappearing during the late 19th century through the mid-20th, first as Pierce’s Disease devastated vineyards and later as Prohibition and rapid urbanization transformed the city into what it is today. Determined to revitalize pieces of this forgotten land, Latta has spent the past several years farming vineyards close to home.

“Riley has spent the last few years focused on farming vineyards closer to home in L.A., including a few years in Anza and, more recently, vines in Malibu directly across the Pacific Coast Highway,” Whalen says. Though Latta is based in L.A., he works with fruit from as far north as Mendocino and as far south as his hometown of Malibu. Working under Jeff Emery, an old-school Pinot Noir producer in the region, and assisting Brent Mayeaux of Stagiaire Wine in his vineyard, Latta is still coming into his own style — in both wine and cider production. But as the identity of contemporary L.A. wines has yet to be defined, Latta’s patient, experimental style of low-intervention winemaking is sure to leave its mark.

Stagiaire Wine

Stagiaire Wine is the project of New Orleans native Brent Mayeaux, named for his time as an apprentice at wineries around the world. Mayeaux began working with more conventionally minded producers in California, but experiences in Australia and France introduced him to natural winemaking through figures like Philippe Bornard in the Jura and Gareth Belton in the Adelaide Hills. In 2018, Mayeaux returned to California with a more French sensibility toward winemaking. It wasn’t until 2021, however, when he shifted his focus to sourcing grapes from high-quality sites, that he truly came into his own.

Today, he makes wine in a former industrial space on Treasure Island, a reclaimed island in the middle of San Francisco Bay — an apt symbol of his idiosyncratic path and distinctive style. Haran McElroy, sommelier at Smithereens, tasted with Mayeaux last year and immediately took note. “Trained in the Jura, based in the Bay Area, Brent Mayeaux a.k.a. Stagiaire makes some of the most sound and joyous wines I’ve had in recent years,” he says. “Working with grapes from high elevation locales in the Santa Cruz mountains, his minimal touch in the cellar on wines like ‘This Slant of Light’ and ‘Sufficiently Whelming’ delivers a new expression of California whites… reaffirming that he’s a winemaker to watch out for in the modern game.”

Scythian Wine Co./Brij Wines/Phelan Farms

There is scarcely a corner of the wine world that Rajat Parr hasn’t mastered. Over the course of his decades-long career, Parr established himself as one of America’s most influential sommeliers, overseeing the wine programs for Michael Mina’s more than 30 restaurants, co-founding San Francisco’s acclaimed RN74, authoring several award-winning books, and helping lead the natural wine movement worldwide. All this before he became one of the most influential winemakers in California today. In his early years as a founding partner and winemaker at Evening Land Vineyards, Sandhi, and Domaine de la Côte, Parr helped drinkers redefine California Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

Recently, he has turned his attention to organic farming on California’s Central Coast, particularly the cool-climate region of Cambria — which was previously essentially untouched by the wine world. Drawing on decades of travel, friendships, and deep wine knowledge, he has introduced extraordinary diversity of grape varieties to the region, including Pink Chardonnay, Trousseau Noir, Savagnin, Jacquère, Gringet, Altesse, Mondeuse, Poulsard, Mencía, alongside the more familiar Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. Over the past decade, Parr has launched Phelan Farm — one of California’s most celebrated new domaines — as well as Brij Wines, which sources organically farmed fruit from the San Luis Obispo Coast, and Scythian Wine Co., focused on the Cucamonga Valley.

Grossman-Weir fell in love with the new guard of California winemakers while working harvest with Raj Parr in Cambria a few years ago. “There is such a community out there of small wineries supporting each other and collaborating to make fresh, carefully made, tiny-production wines.” A gigantic figure in the wine world, Parr’s wines still retain an intimacy and artistry about them that reflects his deep reverence for both the land and its fruit. Though not new to the wine world in any sense, these projects are continuing to push the next generation of California wine into new territories.

content:
Sauvignon Blanc has been here in the U.S. for a long time. From when viticulturist Charles Wetmore, founder of Cresta Blanca Winery, imported original grape cuttings from Bordeaux’s famed Château d’Yquem in the 19th century to when Robert Mondavi coined the rich, oak-aged Fumé Blanc style in Napa Valley.

Since then, the variety has happily existed in California and eventually traveled across the various wine regions of the U.S., from the Pacific Northwest to the shores of Maryland. This year also showed us that Sauvignon Blanc is thriving in Virginia, producing expressive, balanced wines that should not be overlooked in the Savvy B conversation.

We are also witnessing a shift in its home in the Loire Valley of France. The flinty and angular years of the past still exist today, but with more texture and depth. And we must not forget Friuli, a region that embraced stainless steel tanks early, and makes some amazing wines from the grape they call simply Sauvignon.

We tasted all of it for you, and below is our curated compilation of the best of the best from the grapes’ native land to its new terroirs (including Colorado!). Here are the best Sauvignon Blancs of 2026.

Table of Contents

Why You Should Trust VinePair

Every year, VinePair conducts dozens of tastings for our “Buy This Booze” product roundups, highlighting the best bottles across the world’s most popular wine and spirits categories.

Within this scope, VinePair’s tasting and editorial staff sample thousands of bottles every year. This ensures we have a close eye on what’s new and exciting. Crucially, it also provides us with the context needed to distinguish the simply good from the truly great, whether from a quality or value-for-money perspective — or both.

Ultimately, our mission is to offer a clear, reliable source of information for drinkers, providing an overview applicable to day-to-day buying and drinking. Learn more about VinePair’s tastings and reviews department here.

How We Taste

We believe in tasting all products as our readers typically would: with full knowledge of the producer and, importantly, the price. Our tastings are therefore not conducted blind.

VinePair’s tasting panel evaluates every wine on its aromas, flavors, structure, balance, and quality. We also consider whether or not the wine showed typicity for its specific grape or region.

How We Compiled This List

To provide our readers with the most comprehensive and thoroughly tested list of the best Sauvignon Blancs to buy, VinePair invited producers, distributors, and PR firms working on their behalf to send samples for consideration. These bottles were submitted free of charge — producers didn’t pay to submit, nor did VinePair pay for the products. All were requested with the clear understanding that submission does not guarantee inclusion in the final list.

For the Sauvignon Blanc roundup, we assigned a score to each product on a 100-point scale based upon the quality and intensity of its aromas, flavors, texture, and finish. Then we reviewed all scores and compiled an editorially driven list that meets our criteria for the best Sauvignon Blanc to buy right now. Each wine was assessed on quality, price, and availability to compile the final list.

The Best Value Sauvignon Blanc

Dogwood & Thistle Wine Company Monticello Sauvignon Blanc 2025

Owners Sandy and Erin Robertson make great wine. We’ve reviewed many cuvées from Virginia’s Dogwood & Thistle over the years here at VinePair, but this might be the best one yet. Sauvignon Blanc had an amazing vintage in the Commonwealth, with incredible quality that punches far above its price point.

This crisp expression is crafted by gently pressing the grapes and aging the wine in a combination of stainless steel tanks and neutral barrels. This helps maintain freshness while adding a layer of texture and weight to the palate. The wine opens with bright notes of freshly squeezed lemons and white pepper, while the palate delivers ripe orchard fruit and a river rock minerality.

Rating: 94

The Best Splurge Sauvignon Blanc

CHO Wines Sauvignon Blanc 2025

This is an utterly mouth-watering, decadent American Sauvignon Blanc. Based in the Willamette Valley, CHO Wines is best known for its traditional method sparkling wines made with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, but don’t overlook this nuanced take on Sauvignon Blanc. For this wine, the team picks the grapes in two passes, one earlier and one later during harvest, to build complex layers of flavor. The result is a jaw-droppingly beautiful wine.

This bottle pops with vibrant tropical fruit flavors from guava to lychee, with hints of cooking herbs like sage. The mouthfeel is gorgeous, with a compelling waxy texture, ripe fruit, and balanced acidity. While Oregon Sauvignon Blanc might not be on your radar for a splurge, we highly recommend seeking this one out.

Rating: 98

The Best of the Rest:

Best Sauvignon Blancs Under $30

Borgo Conventi Sauvignon 2024

One of the best-kept Italian wine secrets shouldn’t be a secret at all. The Friuli region produces amazing Sauvignon Blanc. One of the first in the country to embrace stainless steel tanks as vessels for fermentation and aging, it makes absolute sense that it would work with this variety. This bright expression of Sauvignon Blanc is a great example. The nose is bold, but not overwhelming, with aromatic notes of jasmine, green bell peppers, and lemon zest. The palate is medium-bodied with ripe stone fruit and citrus notes balanced by supportive acidity.

Stolpman Vineyards Santa Barbara County Sauvignon Blanc 2025

What began as a Napa honeymoon dream in 1974 became reality when Tom and Marilyn Stolpman got the wine bug. They landed in the limestone soils of Ballard Canyon in 1988, an AVA in Santa Barbara that was far less developed than it is today. That pioneering spirit continues today, with the next generation of the Stolpmans running this still family-owned business. This wine is sourced from the Stolpman estate, as well as some low-yielding neighboring vineyards. For the price, you can’t really beat this balance. Crisp and precise, this wine offers notes of passion fruit, guava, fresh herbs, lemon oil, and grapefruit.

Erste + Neue Alto Adige Sauvignon 2025

Erste + Neue (first and new) is a historic co-op in Alto Adige, Italy, formed by the merger of one of the region’s first co-ops with a more modern cooperative. This delicious wine has a fat, juicy nose of sliced apples and bell peppers with hints of freshly cut grass and anise. The palate has an excellent balance with fresh, angular acidity and a rich depth of fruit.

Joseph-Jibril Wines blanc. 2025

Bobby Joseph and Jaam Jibril’s goal with this wine was to make it affordable and easy to sip on an occasion from weeknight to weekend. And they 100 percent achieved that. This Sauvignon Blanc from the Russian River Valley opens with lemon zest, grapefruit pith, juicy pineapple, and jalapeño notes. The mouthful is bright with tangy citrus and a waxy, round texture.

Though not as well-known as its famous neighbors, the Coteaux du Giennois appellation is just north of Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé along the Loire River. This bottle from Vignobles Berthier is made by the fifth generation of the Berthier family and is a wonderful expression of the variety in its perceived home. It brings delicate mineral, floral notes on the nose, with juicy fruit and savory hints on the palate.

Sommeliers Steve Steese and Jayme Henderson decided to leave the dining room to become winemakers in 2017. Did they go to a legacy region like Burgundy, Bordeaux, or even California? No. They set up shop in Colorado. And since then, they have proven that delicious wine can be made there. This unique expression of Sauvignon Blanc delivers notes of guava, juicy apricots, and apples with a distinct minerality. Colorado for the win.

Domaine Vicomte de Noüe-Marinič is a collaboration between local winemaker Alis Marinič and Burgundian nobleman Charles-Louis de Noüe. The idea was to restore abandoned, high-potential vineyards in Slovenia’s Goriška Brda region using Burgundian practices. This Sauvignon has ample depth, with rich notes of citrus, pineapple, and marzipan with fresh herbs. The palate is exceptionally balanced, with a firm grip around the edges and fruit that is aging wonderfully. Drink it now.

Which country makes the best Sauvignon Blanc?

Originally from France, Sauvignon Blanc now grows all over the world. The most notable regions for Sauvignon Blanc are California, New Zealand, Chile, Italy, Bordeaux, the Loire Valley, and South Africa.

Why is New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc so popular?

New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc has notes of tropical fruit, grapefruit, grass, and lime that make the wine easy to sip and appealing to a wide range of tastes. It also pairs well with popular dishes such as seafood and fresh vegetables.

Is Sancerre Sauvignon Blanc?

Sancerre is a region of France that showcases a crisp expression of Sauvignon Blanc grapes. Sauvignon Blanc wines from this region have notes of tart lemon, wet stone, and green apple and are known for their light flavor profile and minerality.

What’s the correct serving temperature for Sauvignon Blanc?

The best serving temperature for Sauvignon Blanc is between 45 and 49 degrees Fahrenheit. A general rule of thumb is that the lighter a wine is in color and flavor, the colder it should be served. We recommend chilling Sauvignon Blanc in the fridge for roughly an hour and a half and letting it come up to temp on the kitchen counter for 20 minutes before serving.

On Tuesday, Maker’s Mark announced the 2026 release of its Cellar Aged series. The fourth edition of this coveted, age-stated collection, Maker’s Mark Cellar Aged 2026 is a combination of 11-, 12-, and 14-year-old bourbons, each bottled at cask-strength and blended to 112.1 proof.

Maker’s Mark first debuted the Cellar Aged series in 2023 with a blend of 11- and 12-year-old bourbons, the brand’s then-oldest release to date. Last year’s release hiked up the age even further to include a 14-year-old bourbon that accounted for 16 percent of the final product. The 2026 release blends 49 percent 11-year-old, 33 percent 12-year-old, and 18 percent 14-year-old bourbons — one of the distillery’s most mature blends to date.

“What excites me isn’t really the numbers — it’s what those different ages contribute to the blend,” Maker’s Mark master distiller Blake Layfield says. “We believe that age is a number, but maturity is a quality. We’re not necessarily chasing the oldest bourbon that we can make. We’re chasing the best flavor that we can create.”

Brand tasting notes highlight dark fruit, clove, and orchard fruit on the nose. The palate opens with a sweetness of honey, brown sugar, and plum flavors, leading into a lingering finish rich in almond, baking spice, and green apple.

Maker’s Mark’s Cellar Aged expressions are aged in a warehouse before finishing maturation in a limestone cavern at the Loretto, Ky., distillery. The site’s traditional warehouses can teeter between -10 degrees Fahrenheit and 120 degrees F, but the cavern maintains a 50 degree F setting, Layfield says. The cellar’s controlled temperature helps Layfield better monitor the whiskeys’ flavor development.

“The lower temperature slows the influence of the wood while allowing the whiskey to continue to evolve,” he says. “That’s how we get that depth and that complexity, while keeping the fruit and oak in balance.”

The newest Cellar Aged release comes as many whiskey brands worldwide are leaning into age-stated expressions. Rather than going full-force into high-age whiskeys, Layfield says, the Cellar Aged blends offer him some elbowroom to experiment with how maturity and youth can interact.

“The 14-year brings extraordinary maturity and depth, but the younger bourbons bring in some of that vibrancy, fruit, and balance,” he says. “Blending is about finding the point where those things start to amplify each other.”

The whiskey will be available at select retailers nationwide starting Sept. 1 for a suggested retail price of $175, with international rollouts to begin later this year and in early 2027.

content:
As in many cities, the cocktail scene is booming in Vilnius, Lithuania, where a growing number of bars are offering world-class mixed drinks, marking a dramatic change from just a decade or so ago. But for some visitors, finding a great Martini can still be a challenge.

Greta Skamaročiūtė, head bartender at Nomads Cocktail Bar in the city’s Old Town, says that several customers have come in with a story to tell. One American couple recently shared what happened when they tried to order their favorite drink elsewhere.

“They mentioned that they went to some other place and asked for a Martini, and the gentleman got a shot of vermouth and a shot of vodka,” she says. “They were quite disappointed with the serve.”

Happily, those travelers found what they wanted at Nomads, where the menu lists five variations on the gin Martini — Dry, Dirty, Gibson, Vesper, and Truffle — among other recipes. For Skamaročiūtė, one of the co-founders of the Baltic Bar Show, it really depends on where you go.

“If it’s a good cocktail bar, you’ll definitely get a good Martini,” she says. “But they’re not in every restaurant, not in every bar, and not on every corner. You have to look for a good place.”

That’s probably true for most drinks, but the Martini seems to be a special case. Today, great options for cocktails abound across Europe, and yet you’ll still find questions about the difficulty of finding a good Martini in online travel and cocktail forums, as well as personal essays from travel writers about how much Continental versions of the drink suck.

It’s not impossible to get a well-chilled, properly stirred combination of gin and vermouth, served up, in the Old World. But for a number of reasons — from brand and ingredient confusion to taste and flavor preferences that cross national borders — it’s still not as easy as it could be.

Different Flavors, Different Strengths

With her dual role as the host of her own cocktail classes and on “My Tiny Bottles,” a podcast and video series on spirits, Tammy Coxen naturally seeks out craft cocktail bars while traveling in Europe, including on a lengthy cross-continental jaunt this summer. One big takeaway? While there are several notable exceptions, Old World drink menus don’t seem to focus on the same “boozy stirred drinks” that fueled the cocktail renaissance in places like New York and San Francisco, and which still get plenty of love in the English-speaking cocktail world.

“When I go to a bar in Europe and I look at the menu, generally speaking, the drinks tend to be on the sweeter side, they tend to have a lot of sours,” she says. “You don’t often see a Martini on the menu.”

The idea that “cocktail” generally means “something fruity, sweet, and sour” seems to cover much of the E.U. at this point, with Martini-focused bars like Barcelona’s iconic Dry Martini being exceptions that prove the rule. Of course, the European continent also includes the U.K., where the Martini has a lengthy tradition, as well as plenty of contemporary buzz, with the Financial Times declaring the dirty version “London’s new It-girl drink” last month. Outside of the British Isles, however, drinkers in Europe seem to prefer very different flavor profiles.

Dieter Moeyaert and Shanna Delfosse are co-owners of Groot Vlaenderen in Bruges, which Gault-Millau recently named Belgium’s “cocktail bar of the year.” Moeyaert says that a classic Martini just isn’t what most customers are looking for.

“The bartenders know it’s a drink, but don’t know it in their bones, and aren’t really sure of the ins and outs of it the way they are with an Aperol Spritz, a Negroni, a Radler, a Picon-Bière, or even a Mojito. It’s just another drink, and not a particularly popular one.”

“I don’t think it’s in our vocabulary when it comes to drinks for the average European,” he says. “It’s definitely not a favorite. I think Europeans usually need a little bit of juice and sugar with their alcohol.” As he sees it, very popular drinks like the Aperol Spritz and the Negroni are “diametrically opposed” to the dry, briny character of a great Martini.

That might be a contemporary preference, but it matches up with history. David Wondrich, author of “The Comic Book History of the Cocktail,” among other titles, points out that Europe never had a multi-decade “Martini cult” the same way as the U.S. did in the mid-20th century. As such, the recipe functions as a kind of “dim memory,” rather than a widely shared cultural touchstone.

“The bartenders know it’s a drink, but don’t know it in their bones, and aren’t really sure of the ins and outs of it the way they are with an Aperol Spritz, a Negroni, a Radler, a Picon-Bière, or even a Mojito,” Wondrich says “It’s just another drink, and not a particularly popular one.” In his experience, modern European craft cocktail bars, century-old institutions, and large hotel bars generally make excellent Martinis. In other venues, the odds might be against you.

Moeyaert says that Groot Vlaenderen generally serves only about one classic Martini per day, usually to someone who is speaking English, not Dutch or French.

“I would say only people from the U.K. and Americans drink it,” he says. “Most Europeans stay away from it, because it’s pretty strong.”

This summer, Moeyaert and Delfosse traveled to the U.K., sampling great Martinis at storied specialty bars like Dukes.“The waft of the alcohol meets you in the lobby as you enter the bar,” he says. “It’s so strong, your day is finished if you have one.”

At Nomads, the relative strength of the Martini has even led to a new menu option. The bar’s five classic Martinis are all made with 60 ml (2.11 oz) of Tanqueray No. 10, which has a relatively brawny 47.3 percent ABV, served in a 6:1 ratio. However, every Martini can also be ordered in a “Tiny” portion, served at half the size, for exactly half the price.

“The main reason was educational, because of course, we noticed it’s not a very popular drink here,” Skamaročiūtė says. “We wanted to have a less intimidating way of drinking a Martini, with an option to try more than one without getting wasted, and without having regrets if you realize the drink is not for you and you just can’t finish it.”

What “Martini” Means

If the wrong taste profile and too much booze are two strikes against the Martini’s popularity in Europe, another might be the power of the Martini brand a.k.a. Martini & Rossi, as well as the widespread tradition of drinking vermouth on its own. Originally founded in Turin, Italy, the company’s vermouth has been a favorite standalone tipple in many European countries for over 150 years. Today, the one-word “Martini” logo is ubiquitous on beach umbrellas, awnings, menus, and table tents across the Continent. As such, if you ask for a Martini at a non-specialist bar, café, or restaurant in many cities, you’re very likely to get a chilled (but not super-cold) glass of Martini Extra Dry, ungarnished, with no other spirit. For a lot of people in Europe, the very word “Martini” means vermouth — not gin, vodka, or something in a V-shaped glass.

The strength of that brand even means that customers are confused about other contemporary drinks with Martini in the name, Delfosse notes.

“It’s definitely not a favorite. I think Europeans usually need a little bit of juice and sugar with their alcohol.”

“A lot of people ask, ‘Is there Martini vermouth in the Pornstar Martini?’” she says. With Groot Vlaenderen’s customers generally looking for “something fruity or more on the sweeter side,” that would be unwelcome, in contrast to the preferences she encountered while sampling Martinis in London this summer. “They like their brine in the U.K.”

In addition, there’s another hermeneutic angle to the Martini’s lack of appeal across Europe. For many, the strength of the drink, its long-term association with James Bond, and lore about the Martini-fueled Rat Pack all combine to cast the Martini in a macho light. By contrast, European cocktail culture can be seen as coming from a very different place.

Or, to quote Dril: This whole thing smacks of gender.

“Martinis in the U.S. were always male-coded, right? It’s men that went out for three-Martini lunches, not women,” Coxen says. “They’re very male-coded, whereas male-coded drinking in Europe is beer. I think that cocktails are more coded ‘women’ in Europe, still, than in North America.”

As such, Skamaročiūtė, Delfosse, and other women in the European drinks industry might be the ones who finally elevate the classic Martini in the Old World. Skamaročiūtė describes the drink as a kind of “final level” for drinkers, who start out by sampling various sweet-and-sour drinks. As an intermediate step, they might move on to the Negroni, whereby they start to appreciate bitterness.

“Then, after you try a lot of things, you can ask for a Martini and actually enjoy it,” she says. “You basically just develop your flavor palate for simpler flavors that are not as loud.”

Delfosse says that a future winter menu at Groot Vlaenderen will feature the Martini more prominently, including a version garnished with blue-cheese-stuffed olives. Her own preference is for a 7:1 ratio, with a dash of orange bitters and a twist.

An olive is acceptable, she says, but no brine, please.

“I love the Martini,” she says. “The dryer, the better.”
